title: Everything I Learned Training Frontier Small Models — Maxime Labonne, Liquid AI

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary object is the frontier small model itself—its architecture, pretraining at 28T tokens, scaling laws, and intrinsic behavioral failure modes like doom looping. The content addresses general-purpose model training and architecture without a specific application vertical. Covers pretraining with 28T tokens, post-training via SFT/DPO/RL, evaluation through benchmarks and doom loop ratios, and deployment via on-device profiling and latency/privacy considerations. Prerequisites include familiarity with transformer architectures, scaling laws, and SFT/DPO/RL pipelines, placing this at an advanced level. Technical conference presentation featuring architecture comparisons, benchmark results, and a detailed training recipe. summary: Maxime Labonne, head of pre-training at Liquid AI, discusses how frontier small models (350M–24B parameters) for on-device deployment differ fundamentally from scaled-down large models. Three defining characteristics are: memory-bound (constrained by phone/car hardware), task-specific (narrow focus rather than general-purpose chat), and latency-sensitive (requiring fast throughput). Architecturally, Labonne critiques models like Gemma 3 270M and Gemma 2.5 0.8B for disproportionately large embedding layers (63% and 29% of parameters respectively), leaving fewer effective parameters for reasoning. LFM2 uses a hybrid architecture with gated short convolutions and GQA, selected through on-device profiling on AMD Ryzen and Samsung Galaxy hardware, achieving faster inference and lower memory than alternatives. The LFM2.5 recipe trains a 350M model on 28T tokens, far exceeding Chinchilla scaling laws but justified by new test-time scaling laws. Post-training stages include narrow SFT, on-policy length-normalized DPO preference alignment, and RL with many environments. Small models are sensitive to cold-start SFT data for RL tasks. A major challenge is doom looping—repetitive output on overly complex tasks. Two mitigation strategies are presented. First, on-policy preference alignment data generation: sampling five temperature rollouts plus one greedy rollout, scoring with an LLM jury, and using doom-loop responses as rejected examples in DPO. Second, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards naturally penalizes non-terminating outputs since no final answer means no positive reward, supplemented by n-gram repetition penalty and temperature-sampled diverse rollouts. Empirically, doom loop ratio on LFM2.5 1.2B thinking was 15-16% after pre-training, barely moved after SFT, dropped significantly after DPO, and became almost nonexistent after RL. By contrast, Qwen 3.5 0.8B in reasoning mode exhibits over 50% doom loops, illustrating it is merely a scaled-down large model. Labonne argues edge models should be treated as their own category with specialized architecture and training. Looking forward, agentic reinforcement learning is the next frontier: web search tools can compensate for low knowledge capacity, and recursive LM environments can address poor long-context capabilities. Small models excel at agentic tasks when given good reasoning and reliable tool use. Labonne concludes that agentic workloads are currently underexplored with small models, and announces LFM 3 is in development.

takeaways: Small models are not scaled-down large models; they are memory-bound, task-specific, and latency-sensitive with unique training challenges.
Large embedding layers in models like Gemma 3 270M (63% of parameters) waste memory that could support more reasoning capacity.
LFM2's gated short convolution blocks, selected via on-device profiling, provide faster inference and lower memory than sliding window attention or gated Delta Net alternatives.
Training a 350M parameter model on 28T tokens exceeds Chinchilla optimality but continues to improve performance per new test-time scaling laws.
Doom looping—repetitive generation on complex tasks—is a critical failure mode for small reasoning models, with SFT insufficient to fix it.
On-policy preference alignment with temperature-sampled rollouts and LLM jury scoring reduces doom loops by rejecting looping responses in DPO.
RL with verifiable rewards naturally penalizes doom loops (no final answer means no reward), reinforced by n-gram repetition penalty and diverse temperature sampling.
Doom loop ratio dropped from 15-16% after pre-training to near-zero after RL, while Qwen 3.5 0.8B exhibits over 50% doom loops in reasoning mode.
Agentic tools like web search and recursive LM environments can compensate for small models' low knowledge capacity and weak long-context capabilities.
Edge models should be treated as a distinct category with specialized architecture and training, not as scaled-down large models.

sections.title: Introduction to frontier small models at Liquid AI
sections.summary: Labonne introduces Liquid AI's focus on edge models from 350M to 24B parameters across text, vision, and audio, with recent releases of VLM 450M and 350M text models on Hugging Face.

sections.title: Characteristics distinguishing small from large models
sections.summary: Three characteristics: memory-bound (hardware constrained), task-specific (narrow focus, not general-purpose chatbots), and latency-sensitive (fast throughput required). Small models are not scaled-down large models.

sections.title: Architecture: embedding layer inefficiency in small models
sections.summary: Gemma 3 270M and Gemma 2.5 0.8B have disproportionately large embedding layers (63% and 29% of parameters) due to distillation from large-vocabulary teachers, reducing effective reasoning parameters.

sections.title: LFM2 architecture: gated short convolutions for speed
sections.summary: LFM2 uses hybrid short convolutions and GQA with a much smaller embedding layer. On-device profiling on AMD Ryzen and Samsung Galaxy hardware shows gated short convolutions are faster and use less memory than alternatives.

sections.title: LFM2.5 training recipe: 28T tokens and post-training stages
sections.summary: LFM2.5 350M trained on 28T tokens, exceeding Chinchilla optimality but justified by new test-time scaling laws. Benchmarks show significant improvement over LFM2 350M on knowledge, instruction following, data extraction, and tool use.

sections.title: Post-training: SFT, preference alignment, and RL best practices
sections.summary: Narrow SFT focus, on-policy length-normalized DPO for general improvement, and RL with many environments. Small models are sensitive to cold-start SFT data matching RL tasks.

sections.title: Identifying and mitigating doom loops in reasoning models
sections.summary: Doom looping—repetitive generation on complex tasks—is a key challenge for small reasoning models. First solution: on-policy preference alignment data generation with temperature-sampled rollouts and LLM jury scoring to reject doom-loop responses.

sections.title: Second doom loop solution: RL with verifiable rewards and repetition penalty
sections.summary: RL with verifiable rewards naturally penalizes doom loops because no final answer means no positive reward. N-gram repetition penalty and temperature-sampled diverse rollouts further reduce looping. Doom loop ratio on LFM2.5 1.2B thinking dropped from 15-16% after pre-training to near-zero after RL, while SFT barely helped. Qwen 3.5 0.8B shows over 50% doom loops, confirming it is merely a scaled-down large model.

sections.title: Future focus: agentic tools to overcome small model limitations
sections.summary: Small models' low knowledge capacity causes hallucination, but web search tools can compensate. Small models excel at agentic tasks given good reasoning and reliable tool use. Recursive LM environments can address weak long-context capabilities. Most small model limitations are fixable with creative, model-specific approaches rather than big-model thinking.

sections.title: Conclusion and Q&A: small vs large model deployment
sections.summary: Labonne concludes that edge models have unique scientific and production challenges, agentic workloads are underexplored with small models, and LFM 3 is in development. In Q&A, he recommends small models for no-internet deployments (in-car), latency-sensitive workloads, and privacy-regulated environments (finance, healthcare). On distilling doom loop fixes from larger models, he is skeptical it would work well, likening it to SFT.
